tagline: Named bends through forest above a river harnessed for aluminum
intro: The Tail of the Dragon is a two-lane stretch of US 129 crossing from Deals Gap into Tennessee. Its eleven Tennessee miles are said to contain 318 curves. The road runs mostly through forest, with a few overlooks and pull-offs; part of it forms the southwestern boundary of Great Smoky Mountains National Park. Copperhead Corner and Gravity Cavity are among the named bends. Across the state line, the route’s street name changes from Tapoco Road to Calderwood Highway, while the US 129 number continues.

The Tail of the Dragon name dates to 1981. Down in the Little Tennessee Valley, an earlier transformation began in 1909, when Alcoa started developing hydroelectric power for its aluminum smelters in Blount County. The camp was established in 1912 and initially called Alcoa; in 1920 it was renamed for engineer I. G. Calderwood, who led the company’s work in the valley. Calderwood Dam began generating in 1930, and the construction camp became a home for dam maintenance crews.

Begin at Deals Gap on the North Carolina-Tennessee line, then follow US 129 into Tennessee through the Dragon’s bends. Calderwood Overlook stands beside US 129 just south of Housley Road, with a view across the reservoir. Housley Road leads down to the surviving Calderwood community buildings on the riverfront.

moments.title: Deals Gap
moments.text: At 1,988 feet, Deals Gap marks the mountain crossing on the North Carolina-Tennessee line beside Great Smoky Mountains National Park. The community with the same name lies 0.7 miles south, at US 129 and NC 28. Motorcyclists and sports-car drivers cross the pass into Tennessee for the Dragon’s curves. US 129 changes its street name across the border, from Tapoco Road in North Carolina to Calderwood Highway in Tennessee. Beyond the pass, the eleven-mile Tennessee stretch runs mostly through forest, with only a few scenic overlooks and places to pull off the highway.

moments.title: Calderwood Overlook
moments.text: The overlook on US 129 faces Calderwood Reservoir, held behind a dam completed in 1930. Alcoa built Calderwood as one of four dams supplying electricity to its aluminum smelting operations in Blount County. The engineering uses a horseshoe bend called the Narrows: the dam occupies the upstream end, while the powerhouse sits downstream. A 2,150-foot concrete tunnel carries diverted river water through the peninsula toward the generating equipment. A smaller dam below the main structure creates a cushion pool that protects the riverbed; the design drew on the action of natural cascades.
moments.notice: The reservoir lies below the US 129 overlook.

moments.title: Calderwood
moments.text: A school and a Quonset-hut theater survive where dam workers once lived. Alcoa established the settlement in 1912 as a base for its Little Tennessee Valley hydroelectric projects. After Calderwood Dam’s completion, maintenance crews replaced construction crews, and the community gained a school and theater in 1950. As the need for onsite crews diminished, residents moved away. The houses were demolished; their foundations and two garages remain alongside the surviving community buildings. The Methodist church remains intact, while the Baptist church has partly collapsed, leaving its front facade. Neither church was included in the dam’s National Register listing.

practical: Calderwood Overlook: The gravel road from the overlook to Calderwood Dam is open only to public foot traffic. (checked 2026-10-11)
Calderwood: Housley Road, the access road to the community structures, is gated at night. (checked 2026-10-11)
